summary.text:
A LOBO story, and an unusually clean one because the council has already decided what it will do. Newcastle holds £141m of LOBO loans. £27m had options called during 2025-26 and were repaid; £23m more carried options before 31 March 2026, and a further £58m have options during 2026-27. The strategy states the policy plainly: if a lender calls, they repay, to reduce refinancing risk in later years.

That means up to £81m of debt could need replacing across about eighteen months, into a curve where ten-year certainty money is around 5.8% and twenty-year around 6.4%. The 2026-27 budget assumes an average interest rate payable of 3.15%, with external interest of £14.6m and MRP of £15.9m.

The liability benchmark is well constructed and worth reading as intended: a Loans CFR of £864.0m at 31 March 2025 less £331.3m of balance sheet resources gives a net loans requirement of £532.7m, and the benchmark peaks at £570.6m in 2027 before falling to £529.5m by 2029. So the borrowing need is front-loaded and then recedes — which is exactly the shape that makes the timing of each LOBO decision matter more than usual. No officer contact is published in this appendix.

contacts.note: No officer named in Appendix B. The strategy delegates execution to the Chief Finance Officer without naming them. Needs the covering report (doc 215900) or another Newcastle paper.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your 2026-27 treasury management strategy. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A note on scope first. We hold 22 PWLB loans for Newcastle at a balance of £377.3m. Your £141m of LOBOs is market debt and sits outside our file entirely, so nothing below claims to tie to it — we only ever hold the PWLB side, and it would be wrong to present that as your whole book.

The LOBOs are why we wrote. £27m called and repaid during 2025-26, £23m carrying options before 31 March 2026, and a further £58m with options during 2026-27. Your strategy states the policy without hedging: if a lender calls, you repay, to reduce refinancing risk later. That is clearer than most and it makes the arithmetic tractable — up to £81m potentially needing replacement across about eighteen months.

What it needs replacing at is the moving part. Ten-year certainty closed at 5.83% this afternoon on notice 314/26 and twenty-year at 6.38%, while your financial implications section assumes an average interest rate payable of 3.15% for the 2026-27 budget, with external interest of £14.6m and MRP of £15.9m. Those two numbers are not in conflict — a 3.15% average across the whole book is entirely consistent with replacement money costing nearly twice that at the margin — but the gap is what determines how much of the £81m matters to the revenue position, and it changes with the curve rather than with the reporting cycle.

We have now picked up five LOBO calls across the sector in a few months — Kent, Tameside, York, Barnet and your own £27m — and the pattern is consistent: lenders testing options now that PWLB rates have risen far enough to make the embedded option worth exercising. That is a cross-council picture no council can see from its own papers, and it is exactly the sort of thing we publish. It also suggests the £58m with options during 2026-27 is more likely to be tested than not, though we would not put it stronger than that.

Your liability benchmark is worth reading as intended and we did. Loans CFR of £864.0m at 31 March 2025 less £331.3m of balance sheet resources gives a net loans requirement of £532.7m; the benchmark peaks at £570.6m in 2027 and recedes to £529.5m by 2029. A front-loaded need that then falls away is precisely the shape in which the timing of each LOBO decision carries most weight, because replacing at the peak locks in a rate you may not need for the full term.

One thing from our own data. All 22 of your PWLB loans price below par on the DMO's premature repayment curve today — not one in premium, which is unusual even in a year like this — for about £169.6m of discount against the £377.3m balance. We're not suggesting anything follows from it: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP and no accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Ours is indicative and the page says so. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

For the replacement side, our monthly sector breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, which is a thin market to be entering with £58m.

On training, four fit Newcastle. LOBO loans (legacy) is written for exactly this. Debt restructuring sits alongside it. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice, given yours is better built than most and repays being used rather than just reported. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
